title: How does Kosovo keep the lights on?
Here is its electricity system, by the numbers.
coal: Almost all of it starts in Obilitch, just outside Prishtina.
Two lignite plants, Kosovo A, and Kosovo B,
burn coal from the open-pit mine next door.
In twenty twenty-five, they made eighty-eight percent of the country's power.
old: Kosovo A's working units date from the nineteen seventies. Kosovo B's, from the eighties.
Last year, unit B two ran just fifty-six percent of the time.
Total output fell by almost thirteen percent.
gap: Many homes heat with electricity, so cold evenings push the grid to its limit.
On New Year's Eve, demand hit a record: one thousand six hundred and twenty-four megawatts.
All the working plants together add up to about one thousand two hundred and sixty.
imports: The rest comes over the border.
In twenty twenty-five, Kosovo imported almost two thousand gigawatt hours,
forty-two percent more than the year before.
After exports, that covered about twenty-three percent of demand.
And it is costly: roughly two hundred and fifty million euros in eleven months.
res: At the end of twenty twenty-five, Kosovo had one hundred and thirty-seven megawatts of wind,
one hundred and twenty-nine of hydro,
Together they made about twelve percent of Kosovo's own generation.
In twenty twenty-six, the seventy megawatt Zatrich wind farm joined them.
plan: The plan runs to twenty thirty-one.
Thirty-five percent of electricity from renewables.
Six hundred megawatts of wind, six hundred of solar,
and batteries: at least one hundred and seventy megawatts.
Renewable capacity has to grow about five times in six years.
Auctions have begun. The first solar park won at under forty-nine euros per megawatt hour.
hurdles: Three things stand in the way.
One: the plan is to repair the old coal units and keep them running. Coal ends by twenty fifty at the latest.
Two: Kosovo has no carbon price, while the European Union now charges a carbon levy on imported electricity.
Three: the national energy and climate plan was still a draft in mid twenty twenty-six.
outro: and the next six years decide whether wind, sun and batteries can take over.
